title: Enzyme Activation and Reserve Mobilization
objective: Explain how a germinating cannabis embryo restarts metabolism and converts stored reserves into usable energy and building materials.

terms.definition: Conversion of stored lipids, proteins, or carbohydrates into transportable metabolites.
An enzyme that breaks chemical bonds using water.
Cellular pathways that release usable energy from organic molecules.
Plant pathway that helps convert stored lipids into carbon compounds supporting seedling growth.

coreScience: The dry embryo contains stored molecules, organelles, messenger RNAs, enzymes, and protective systems prepared during maturation. Hydration does not simply 'wake up one enzyme.' It permits coordinated repair, translation, respiration, and synthesis across many cells and tissues.

Measured hemp seed lots contain substantial oil reserves, although composition varies among genotypes. Their early reserve use is therefore described with the general oilseed model: stored lipids are mobilized through beta-oxidation and related carbon-conversion pathways, while proteins and carbohydrates also contribute. The pathway is conserved plant physiology, not direct proof that every step has been quantified in cannabis seedlings. Cotyledons later become photosynthetically active after emergence.

Reserve mobilization supports radicle growth, hypocotyl extension, cell-wall production, and the transition to autotrophic growth. Slow germination can reflect low temperature, seed deterioration, oxygen limitation, dormancy, or damage; it should not be explained as a vague lack of 'enzymes' without evidence.

Reserve use changes as the seedling transitions from heterotrophic dependence on stored compounds toward autotrophic growth. Lipid-rich reserves can be converted into respiratory substrates and structural carbon, while stored proteins supply amino acids and mineral nutrients are redistributed internally. As cotyledons expand and photosynthesis increases, the relative importance of external light rises and dependence on internal reserves declines. A delayed seedling can therefore reflect problems in several linked processes rather than one missing enzyme or nutrient.
cultivationRelevance: A viable seed normally carries reserves for the earliest germination stages; external fertilizer does not replace reserve mobilization. Cannabis salinity responses are treatment-dependent, and a sodium-chloride study is not a universal fertilizer-rate study. Replace the undefined instruction 'heavy feeding' with a controlled comparison: record solution composition, pH, and EC, and compare early growth with an untreated or lower-salinity condition.
Protect the process by stabilizing temperature, water availability, oxygen, and sanitation. Correct the environment before adding unverified stimulants.

During the earliest stages, prioritize conditions that allow the seed to use its own reserves: adequate water, oxygen, temperature, and sanitation. Adding stronger nutrient solution cannot compensate for a dead embryo or severely impaired reserve mobilization and may increase osmotic stress.

When testing a priming product, stimulant, sugar, or nutrient treatment, use an untreated control and separate outcomes: time to radicle emergence, final germination, abnormal seedlings, emergence, and later growth. A treatment that speeds one endpoint may not improve final establishment.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record lot ID, harvest/receipt age, baseline germination, known storage temperature/moisture history, and any prior deterioration or rescue treatment. Reserve-mobilization interpretations depend on starting seed quality.

Record temperature, moisture method, aeration/oxygen-risk conditions, medium, light exposure after emergence, and contamination. These factors can alter respiration and growth independently of reserve quantity.

Record radicle protrusion, hypocotyl emergence, cotyledon opening/greening, first true leaves, and time to each stage. This shows where the transition from stored-reserve dependence to active photosynthesis may be delayed.
Record root development, cotyledon size/color, symmetry, lesions, elongation, true-leaf development, and survival. Keep abnormal categories separate from simple delay.
For priming, additives, sugars, or nutrient exposure, record concentration/composition, pH/EC where relevant, duration, sample size, matched untreated control, and all germination/seedling endpoints.

State whether the evidence supports delayed metabolism, environmental limitation, deterioration, treatment effect, or unresolved cause. Avoid attributing slow germination to a vague enzyme deficiency without direct evidence.

misconceptions: Fertilizer powers germination: Early germination is powered primarily by stored reserves and respiration.
One additive activates all seeds: Response depends on viability, dormancy, damage, environment, and treatment.
Large seeds always make superior adults: Seed reserves can affect establishment, but later phenotype depends on genetics and environment.
evidenceLimits: Core reserve-mobilization pathways are well established in general oilseed and seed physiology, but quantitative pathway activity has not been mapped for every cannabis genotype or germination condition. Hemp seed composition also varies among genotypes. Changes in germination speed after priming or nutrient exposure do not identify which metabolic step changed unless the mechanism is measured directly, so production interpretation should remain outcome-based.
